opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I spent a fair amount of time poking at, and the honest answer is that at small scale, ResNets are really hard to beat for Go.

The intuition is that a Go board is a 19-by-19 grid where a lot of what matters is local: shapes, liberties, whether a group is connected to its neighbor. Convolutions bake that inductive bias directly into the architecture. Translation equivariance, locality, weight sharing across the board: you get all of that for free. So when you don't have a ton of self-play games or a big GPU budget, the ResNet just learns faster per sample and per FLOP. It doesn't have to discover that adjacent intersections matter more than distant ones. It's told that up front.

Transformers, by contrast, start out pretty agnostic. Every position can attend to every other position from layer one. That's powerful, because Go does have long-range dependencies. Ladders are the classic example, and so is life-and-death that depends on a group way across the board. But the model has to spend data learning the spatial structure that the conv net already assumes. In the low-data regime, that shows up as worse sample efficiency and often less stable training. You end up fiddling with positional encodings, learning rates, warmup, all that stuff, just to get parity.

What I found, and I think this matches the broader lore, is that the crossover point where transformers start to win is further out than people expect for a domain like this. If you're a hobbyist or a small lab trying to train a decent Go bot, I'd just use a ResNet, something KataGo-style with global pooling layers to patch over the long-range weakness. That pooling trick gets you a lot of the "global context" benefit without paying the transformer tax.

Where transformers get interesting is if you're scaling way up, or if you want one architecture that transfers across lots of games or modalities. Then the generality starts paying for itself. But for "I have a few GPUs and a weekend," the conv net is the pragmatic choice. It's a nice little case study in how inductive bias is basically a substitute for data.

r001.rationale: The response says that in the speaker’s experience, ResNets are hard to beat for Go at small scale and recommends them when games and GPU budget are limited.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I think about a lot because the small-budget regime is where most people actually live. Nobody outside of DeepMind or a handful of labs is training on millions of self-play games with thousands of TPUs.

My honest take is that for Go specifically, at small scale, ResNets are still really hard to beat, and the reason is inductive bias. A Go board is a 19 by 19 grid, and the rules are fundamentally local. Liberties, captures, whether a group is alive or dead, these are all things that are determined by what's happening in a neighborhood of stones. A convolution is basically the perfect prior for that. You get translation equivariance for free, so a shape you learn in the corner transfers to the other corner without the network having to see it in every position. That's a huge data multiplier when you only have, say, a hundred thousand games.

A transformer has to learn all of that from scratch. It has to figure out from attention patterns that stone at position 3,4 cares about stone at 3,5. With enough data it absolutely will, and it'll probably learn some things the ResNet struggles with, like long-range ladder reading or whole-board influence judgments that span across the board. But in the low-data regime it's spending a lot of its capacity rediscovering locality, and that's capacity you could have spent on actually learning Go.

The compute side has the same story. Attention is quadratic in the number of positions, and 361 tokens isn't huge, but for a given FLOP budget you're getting fewer effective parameter updates than you'd get with a convnet that's doing cheap 3 by 3 ops. So you train slower and you have less data to begin with. That's a bad combination.

Now, the thing I'd caveat is that there's a middle ground that I think is actually the right answer for most people, which is a ResNet backbone with a little bit of global context mixed in. KataGo does something like this with global pooling layers, where you take the whole-board feature map, pool it down, and broadcast it back so every position gets a summary of the global state. That gets you most of what you'd want from attention, which is awareness of things like ko fights happening elsewhere or overall territory count, without paying the data cost of learning locality from nothing.

And then if your budget grows, that's when I'd start swapping in attention blocks, maybe in the later layers where the features are already abstracted, and see if the extra flexibility pays off. The general pattern I've seen across a bunch of domains, not just Go, is that the inductive bias wins when you're data-starved and the flexibility wins when you're data-rich. The transition point is a lot further out than people expect for board games because the structure is so clean.

So short version: small budget, use a ResNet, add global pooling, don't overthink it. The transformer is the thing you reach for when you've already scaled the ResNet and it's stopped improving.

r001.rationale: He says that for Go at small scale, ResNets are “still really hard to beat,” and frames this as his own take and experience.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the architecture question from the scaling question. Transformers have been incredibly successful, but that doesn’t mean they’re the best choice at every data and compute budget.

For Go, a ResNet has a useful inductive bias: the same local patterns matter in different parts of the board. Convolutions build that assumption in, so the network doesn’t have to learn it entirely from examples. When data is scarce, that can be a substantial advantage. And with a small compute budget, a well-tuned ResNet is a very strong baseline.

A transformer makes it easier to connect distant parts of the board, which is useful because Go certainly isn’t just a local game. But that flexibility doesn’t automatically translate into better performance at small scale. You have to compare actual playing strength at the same training cost and inference budget. In a search-based player, a cheaper network can also let you search more.

So my default at small budgets would be a ResNet. I’d want evidence from a controlled comparison before switching to a transformer, rather than assuming that the architecture that wins at enormous scale also wins in this regime.

r001.rationale: The response favors ResNets as the default at small budgets, but does not report that this is Eric Jang’s experience or state that ResNets tend to outperform transformers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is how much structure you have to learn from data. A ResNet gives you locality and translation equivariance almost for free. Those are useful priors for Go: a lot of the same tactical patterns show up in different places on the board. If your data and compute budgets are small, you probably want to exploit that structure rather than spend capacity rediscovering it.

A transformer gives you a more direct way to connect distant parts of the board, which is attractive because Go has these global dependencies. But that flexibility doesn’t necessarily make it more sample efficient. And on a small board, a sufficiently deep convolutional network can already propagate information across the whole board.

So my default under tight budgets would be a ResNet. I’d be interested in a transformer or a hybrid, but I’d want to compare them at equal total compute—including the self-play needed to generate the training data—and measure playing strength, rather than just prediction accuracy.

r001.rationale: The response favors a ResNet under tight budgets, but presents this as a default based on architectural considerations and a proposed comparison. It does not report that, in Eric Jang’s experience, ResNets tend to outperform transformers.
